la:noun:hydra.html:
Hȳdra, ae, f., = Ὕδρα [kindred with Sanscr. udri; Ang.-Sax. oter, otor; Engl. and Germ. Otter; cf. also the Gr. ἔνυδρις],
the water-serpent killed by Hercules near the Lernean Lake, the Hydra, with seven heads; as fast as one of them was cut off two sprang up in its stead; it is also called Echidna: Lernaea pestis, Hydra,; ; ; ; ; ; . As identified with Echidna, the mother of Cerberus, Cic. poët. Tusc. 2, 9, 22.—Prov.: vide ne in istis duobus generibus hydra tibi sit et pellis, Hercules autem et alia opera majora, in illis rebus, quas praetermittis, relinquantur,i. e. the easiest, the least important,.—
Deriv. Hȳdraeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Hydra: germen,.—
Transf.
The constellation of the Water-snake, also called Anguis, (also ); ; .—
Acc. to Verg., a hydra with fifth heads, that keeps watch at the gates of the Lower World, .

la:noun:hydrus.html:
hydrus or -os, i, m., = ὕδρος,
a water-serpent, serpent (cf.: chelydrus, chersydrus, anguis, serpens).
Lit., ; ; ; : marini,. In the hair of the Furies, of Medusa, etc., ; ; ; hence poet. transf.: nam si Vergilio puer et tolerabile desit Hospitium, caderent omnes a crinibus hydri, i. e. all his poetic fire would have come to naught (referring to his description of the Furies, A. 7, 415 and 447), .—
Transf.
The poison of a serpent, .—
Hydros, i, the constellation of the Waterserpent, called also Anguis and Hydra, .

la:noun:hyacinthus.html:
Hўăcinthus or -os, i, m., = Ὑάκινθος,
a beautiful Spartan youth, son of Œbalus, beloved by Apollo, and accidentally killed by a blow of his quoit; from his blood sprang the flower of the same name, marked with the exclamation AI, ; ; ; .—Plur.: sed gladiator erat; facit hoc illos Hyacinthos,i. e. as beautiful as Hyacinthus,.—
Hўăcinthĭa, ōrum, n., the festival in honor of Hyacinthus, in Sparta, .—
Hence, hўăcinthus or -os, i, m., the hyacinth, not, however, our hyacinth, but either the blue iris or fleur-delis, Iris Germanica, Linn.; the corn-flag or gladiolus, Gladiolus communis, Linn.; or the rocket larkspur, Delphinium Ajacis, Linn.; ; ; ; ; ; Col. poët. 10,100.—Hence,
Transf., f., a precious stone of the color of a hyacinth (perh. our sapphire or a dark-colored amethyst), ; ; .

la:noun:hypocrita.html:
hўpocrĭta or -es, ae, m., = ὑποκριτής.
A mime who accompanied the delivery of an actor by gestures, ; ; .—
In eccl. Lat., a hypocrite, ; ;
